title: A shelf-stable oxygen carrier that can replace donor red cells in hemorrhage

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an oxygen-carrying product that can be stored without refrigeration and administered during life-threatening bleeding to perform the oxygen-delivery function of donor red cells. It would need to work at the volumes and repeat doses that resuscitation requires, with acceptable safety, and without blood-type matching. The target is a clinically effective replacement for red-cell oxygen delivery when donor blood is unavailable or delayed; the supplied evidence does not establish that this combined capability has been achieved.

Hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers are a major route toward this goal. Hemoglobin normally carries oxygen inside red cells, but earlier products using purified hemoglobin outside those cells encountered serious toxicity. Researchers have explored chemical cross-linking, polymerization, lipid encapsulation, and recombinant modification to improve performance. These approaches are documented in the supplied review's abstract and retained figure-caption text, but their exploration does not establish that any design meets the full clinical and storage requirements.

Scope clarification: replacing red-cell oxygen delivery is narrower than replacing whole blood. An oxygen carrier would not itself seal a bleeding vessel, supply platelets or clotting factors, or remove the need for surgery and other bleeding-control measures. The concept belongs primarily to emergency clinical medicine, with enabling work in protein engineering, biomaterials, and pharmaceutical formulation.

significance.text: Donor-dependent transfusion has substantial logistical constraints. The supplied review identifies reliance on volunteer donors, supply shortages, short storage life, possible infectious transmission, and immune complications, with many limitations more severe in low-income countries. These constraints explain why a safe alternative could matter even where donor red cells are already effective when available promptly.

Conditional impact assessment: a safe, shelf-stable product that requires no type matching could make oxygen delivery available closer to the point of bleeding, including during transport or in facilities with limited blood-banking capacity. Its revolutionary feature would be access and deployment: preserving a resuscitation option when donor red cells cannot arrive in time. That impact depends on demonstrated efficacy, storage reliability, sufficient supply, and practical administration, rather than on oxygen-carrying capacity alone.

Potential downstream uses include trauma care, obstetric hemorrhage, and remote or resource-constrained emergency care. These are plausible applications, not established benefits across those populations. Use by patients who refuse donor blood would also depend on the product's composition and individual acceptance. A successful carrier could complement bleeding control and coagulation support, but it would not make them unnecessary or establish superiority over promptly available donor red cells.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is the combination of useful oxygen delivery, acceptable safety at resuscitation doses, and shelf stability. The review describes hypertension caused by vasoconstriction and multiple organ toxicities with early purified native hemoglobin. It attributes these effects partly to nitric-oxide scavenging, reactive oxygen species, and possible sterile inflammation. Later large clinical trials continued to encounter elevated adverse-event rates, failure to meet specified clinical endpoints, or both.

Engineering synthesis: a candidate must carry and release enough oxygen to improve tissue oxygenation while avoiding effects on vascular tone and organ function that undermine that benefit. Chemical modification, polymerization, encapsulation, and recombinant redesign offer different ways to alter hemoglobin's behavior, but the supplied evidence does not establish which approach, if any, resolves the clinical tradeoffs. Repeated administration and clinically necessary volumes are requirements to test, not dose-specific capabilities demonstrated by this record.

Engineering synthesis: storage must preserve both oxygen-delivery performance and safety throughout a specified unrefrigerated shelf life. Success therefore requires more than a promising freshly manufactured formulation: manufacture, storage, transport, and administration must yield a consistent product. Whether encapsulated hemoglobin or a design outside the cell-free hemoglobin approach can avoid earlier toxicities remains unresolved by the supplied evidence; those earlier failures do not prove that every alternative must fail.

current_state.text: The sole supplied scientific source is Youmna Abdelghany and colleagues' review, “Artificial Oxygen Carriers: Lessons From Hemoglobin-Based Oxygen Carrier Clinical Trials and Current Development Efforts,” published online on September 12, 2025, and in the March 1, 2026 issue of Shock, volume 65(3), pages 374–389. It summarizes decades of development of cell-free hemoglobin products as potential substitutes for red-cell transfusion. It reports promising preliminary findings alongside large clinical trials with elevated adverse events and/or failure to meet specified endpoints. This supports continued investigation and a substantial unresolved safety-and-efficacy barrier, rather than an achieved replacement capability.

The review reports that no hemoglobin-based oxygen carrier had obtained US Food and Drug Administration approval for clinical use. This is a statement in the review's publication context, not an independently verified regulatory update through November 2026. Its retained Figure 2 caption documents cross-linking, polymerization, lipid encapsulation, and recombinant modification as development approaches; the supplied review does not establish that any one approach has demonstrated the complete capability described here.

The available evidence is the supplied PubMed record, including its abstract, retained figure captions, and conflict-of-interest disclosures. The full review and figure images were not inspected in the supplied assessment. Several authors disclose relevant commercial roles, shareholdings, or patents involving heme-based therapeutics and artificial oxygen carriers. These disclosures provide context for interpreting the review; they do not by themselves invalidate its findings.

The retained PubMed record exposes only a subset of the review's 187 references. It therefore does not verify the earlier assertion that this review cites a particular 2008 meta-analysis of death and myocardial infarction, and no risk ratios from that analysis can be carried forward from the supplied evidence. The reference-display limitation is not evidence that the full review omits the analysis. Foreign licensure and named expanded-access products also remain unverified here.

Evidence boundary: the source was retrieved on November 1, 2026, but retrieval of an older review does not establish coverage of developments up to that date. No freshness-search record was supplied. The materials consequently leave subsequent trials, regulatory changes, and the present performance of alternative designs unassessed; this gap does not contradict the review's dated clinical summary.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: randomized trials in life-threatening hemorrhage, in settings where immediate donor red cells are limited or delayed, should show that the product supports survival and reversal of shock at least as well as the available standard. Trial designs should specify clinically justified efficacy and safety margins in advance and assess death, myocardial infarction, and severe organ injury. These are proposed criteria for this concept, not established standards endorsed by the supplied review.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized trials demonstrate comparable hemorrhage survival and shock reversal

completion_criteria.text: Proposed dosing and storage demonstration: the product should remain effective and acceptably safe at clinically necessary volumes and repeat doses, rather than only after a small initial exposure. It should have a validated shelf life under explicitly specified conditions that do not require refrigeration, with retained performance and safety through the claimed storage period. Administration without type matching should be demonstrated within a clearly defined intended-use population.
completion_criteria.label: Effective resuscitation dosing with validated unrefrigerated storage and unmatched administration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: convincing evidence should extend across manufacturing lots, clinical sites, and representative patients, with transparent reporting of adverse events, concurrent resuscitation treatments, and circumstances in which the product fails or should not be used. Evidence from one hemorrhage setting should not automatically be generalized to trauma, obstetric bleeding, every age group, or all comorbidities. Finite trials can establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible clinical evidence with reported harms and applicability limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope threshold: veterinary approval, individual-patient expanded access, improved laboratory oxygen measurements, or preliminary safety findings alone would not demonstrate replacement of donor red-cell oxygen delivery in life-threatening human hemorrhage. Clinical benefit must be shown alongside the storage and administration capabilities. Bleeding control and coagulation support remain part of care even if the oxygen carrier succeeds.
completion_criteria.label: Human hemorrhage benefit demonstrated alongside storage and administration capabilities

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with the supplied roster: CLM-05, “Durable organ xenotransplantation at clinical scale,” and CLM-11, “Implantable human-scale organs assembled outside the body,” share the aim of reducing dependence on scarce donated biological resources. CLM-14 instead seeks an acutely administered oxygen-delivery product. It does not require a living organ to integrate and function durably after implantation, so their clinical endpoints and engineering barriers remain distinct.

Conceptual comparison: CLM-06, “Therapeutic remuscularization of the adult human heart,” and CLM-15, “Restoration of nephron number in the adult human kidney,” address lasting tissue restoration. CLM-14 seeks temporary physiological support during an emergency. Avoiding cardiac and renal injury is an important safety requirement for an oxygen carrier, but delivering oxygen or avoiding injury does not itself regenerate heart muscle or nephrons.

Conceptual comparison: CLM-01, “Programmable antigen-specific immune tolerance,” overlaps with the broad concern of immune compatibility. However, giving an oxygen carrier without blood-type matching would not establish programmed immune tolerance or eliminate every possible immune reaction. CLM-09, “Curative in vivo genome writing beyond the liver,” shares a broad connection to molecular engineering, but recombinant redesign of a manufactured carrier is distinct from editing a patient's genome. These roster entries retain separate identities and completion criteria.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not identify a product that meets the combined hemorrhage-efficacy, safety, dosing, type-matching, and unrefrigerated-storage requirements.
Regulatory status and clinical developments after the review's publication context remain unassessed; foreign licensure and named expanded-access products are not verified.
The full review, figure images, and complete reference list were not inspected in the supplied assessment. The claimed 2008 meta-analysis citation and its quantitative results remain unverified.
It remains unresolved whether a particular modified, encapsulated, or alternative oxygen-carrier design can avoid earlier toxicities at clinically necessary volumes and repeat doses.

Specific shelf-life duration, storage-temperature range, dosing regimen, trial margins, and intended-use populations require product-specific justification; none is established by the supplied materials.

brief.title: An oxygen-carrying substitute for donor red blood cells
possible: Someone bleeding heavily could receive an oxygen-carrying fluid when donor red blood cells cannot arrive in time. It could be kept without refrigeration and given without matching blood types, including at the large volumes and repeated doses needed during emergency care.
why: Ambulance crews and hospitals with limited blood supplies could keep oxygen delivery within reach. This could help people with severe injuries or bleeding during childbirth, especially where blood banks are scarce.

sources.showed: Their review describes efforts to use hemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying protein in red cells, outside those cells. Early products caused high blood pressure and organ damage; larger trials continued to find harm or missed treatment goals.
sources.quote: Despite some promising results in preliminary studies, large-scale clinical trials have continued to show elevated rates of adverse events and/or a failure to meet specified clinical endpoints.
sources.cited_for: Past human trials expose the central challenge of delivering oxygen without causing serious harm.
sources.not_established: The review does not establish a safe, effective replacement that also meets the dosing and storage requirements.

sources.who: Masahiro Tokuno, Kazuaki Taguchi and colleagues
sources.showed: In rats with severe blood loss, stored hemoglobin enclosed in tiny fat membranes supported recovery comparably to fresh red cells, without the lung injury associated with older stored red cells.
sources.quote: The six-hour mortality after resuscitation was not significantly different among the groups.
sources.cited_for: Stored carriers retained useful oxygen-delivery performance in an animal experiment.
sources.not_established: An animal experiment does not establish survival benefit or safety at the volumes and repeated doses needed in people.

sources.showed: In a small dog study, membrane-enclosed hemoglobin restored blood pressure and oxygen delivery after severe bleeding following removal of a lung. It performed better than a protein fluid without the carrier.
sources.quote:
Oxygen delivery was restored in the HbV group 
and was significantly higher than that in the HSA group (P < 0.0001).
sources.cited_for: The carrier supported oxygen delivery despite blood loss and reduced lung function.
sources.not_established: This small animal study did not establish benefit in human bleeding or equivalence to donor red cells.

shown: Tokuno and colleagues found that a carrier stored for a year supported recovery after severe bleeding in rats comparably to fresh red cells. Nakano and colleagues restored oxygen delivery in dogs after lung removal and blood loss. Human trials of earlier hemoglobin products have faced serious safety problems.
missing: Human trials have yet to establish comparable survival and recovery with acceptable risks of heart attack and severe organ injury.
A product must combine safe emergency volumes and repeated doses with proven unrefrigerated storage and use without blood-type matching.
Reliable results must extend across production batches, hospitals and clearly defined patient groups.

milestones.label: Comparable survival and recovery after severe bleeding
milestones.explanation: Randomized trials would have to show comparable survival and reversal of shock, when circulation cannot meet the body's needs, with acceptable harm. This would establish benefit when donor red cells are delayed.

milestones.label: Effective repeated dosing after storage without refrigeration
milestones.explanation: The carrier would have to remain effective and acceptably safe at emergency volumes and repeat doses after its claimed unrefrigerated shelf life, without blood-type matching. This would establish practical emergency use.

milestones.label: Repeatable clinical results with clear limits and harms
milestones.explanation: Results would have to hold across production batches, hospitals and representative patients, with harms, accompanying treatments and failures reported. This would define whom the carrier can reliably help.

milestones.label: Human benefit combined with storage and administration capabilities
milestones.explanation: Human bleeding trials would have to demonstrate benefit alongside storage and administration capabilities. This would establish replacement of red-cell oxygen delivery; bleeding control and support for clotting would remain necessary.

uncertain: It remains unclear which carrier design can avoid earlier toxic effects at the volumes and repeated doses needed during severe bleeding.
Storage conditions, shelf life, dosing and acceptable trial margins need justification for each product.
Benefits in one bleeding setting may not extend to childbirth, other ages or people with other illnesses.

page.title: Shelf-stable oxygen therapeutics for hemorrhage
page.definition: An intravenous fluid carries oxygen to tissues during life-threatening hemorrhage when donor red cells are unavailable. Its labelled storage conditions allow stocking without refrigeration, and it can be given without matching the patient's blood group. It supplies the oxygen-delivery function of red cells. Platelets and clotting factors serve separate functions. Hemopure, made from the oxygen-carrying protein hemoglobin, already keeps at room temperature for at least three years. Its South African approval covers acute anemia in adult surgical patients, and its US use remains investigational.

goal.need: In US emergency medical services records for 2020–2023, only 2,289 of 262,761 injured patients who met a vital-sign screen for possible transfusion received blood before hospital arrival. Donor red cells in additive solutions ordinarily keep for 42 days at 1–6 °C. Where crews cannot maintain refrigeration, a safe oxygen carrier could support a bleeding patient's tissues during transport until donor red cells are available. Patients still need bleeding control and may need platelets and clotting factors.

statements.body: DARPA, Resuscitation and Prevention of Ischemia-Induced Dysfunction (RAPIID) programme
statements.quote: RAPIID will advance synthetic, shelf-stable blood components through clinical trials, regulatory approval, manufacturing scale-up, and the development of ruggedized fielding technologies.
statements.context: The programme includes stand-alone oxygen carriers alongside platelet products and dried plasma.

statements.body: Institute of Medicine, Committee on Fluid Resuscitation for Combat Casualties
statements.quote: delivery in the wounded subject for 24 to 48 hours.
statements.context: Recommendation 4.1 of Fluid Resuscitation calls for evaluating small-volume, stable agents that carry oxygen or facilitate its delivery. The 24 to 48 hours refers to the duration of oxygen support after injury.

completion.title: An oxygen therapeutic gains FDA approval for hemorrhage with unrefrigerated storage.
completion.criterion: FDA approves or licenses an oxygen therapeutic for oxygen-delivery support during life-threatening human hemorrhage when donor red cells are unavailable. The approved indication, administration instructions and stability-supported labeling must cover use without blood-group matching and storage without refrigeration. The approved dose and any repeat dosing define the demonstrated replacement capacity; storage temperature and expiry remain product-specific.
completion.set_by: US Department of Health and Human Services/BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels for Medical Countermeasure Products, criterion 8C; applied to the indication and storage capability defined here.
completion.basis: HHS/BARDA uses FDA approval or licensure as its threshold and requires stability studies to support labelled expiry. The indication, dose and storage conditions belong to the individual product. Fluosol's US approval covered myocardial ischemia during coronary angioplasty. Hemopure has South African approval for acute anemia in adult surgical patients and remains investigational in the US, including under expanded access. FDA withdrew its oxygen-therapeutics draft guidance on 8 May 2015.

milestones.title: An oxygen therapeutic demonstrates preliminary efficacy in a living-animal hemorrhage model.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate preliminary efficacy of the candidate as a resuscitation fluid in a living-animal model of hemorrhage. Good Laboratory Practice compliance is not required for this proof-of-concept study.
milestones.set_by: HHS/BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels, criterion 3C.
milestones.threshold_quote: Generate preliminary in vivo proof-of-concept efficacy data

milestones.title: An oxygen carrier meets RAPIID’s 10% performance margin and six-month storage test.
milestones.criterion: Meet RAPIID’s preclinical tests: safety and efficacy within a 10% margin of the comparable blood component; non-toxicity and pharmacological safety in IND-enabling assessments; and at least six months’ storage at sustained 4°C, 25°C and 40°C with no more than 10% change in physicochemical characteristics and functionality versus composition-matched unstored product. Government-chosen final packaging must additionally pass at least three months at those temperatures. These are programme metrics, not human clinical noninferiority margins.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, RAPIID solicitation DARPA-PS-26-124, Amendment 1, section 2.3.2.1 and Table 2; metrics for individual blood analog components.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate ≥6 months shelf-stability at 4, 25, and 40°C with ≤10% difference in physicochemical characteristics and functionality vs. fresh product

milestones.title: A regulator permits an oxygen therapeutic to enter a human clinical trial.
milestones.criterion: Meet the regulatory and ethics requirements to begin the human investigation in its jurisdiction. In the US, an Investigational New Drug application takes effect 30 days after FDA receipt unless FDA imposes a clinical hold, or earlier if FDA authorizes the investigation to begin. Institutional review board approval is also required. An investigation under the emergency research exception from informed consent requires prior written FDA authorization.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.40 and 312.20(c), for the US route.
milestones.threshold_quote: Thirty days after FDA receives the IND

milestones.title: An oxygen therapeutic completes an initial human safety and pharmacokinetic assessment.
milestones.criterion: Complete one or more phase 1 trials that establish initial human safety and pharmacokinetics for the candidate, with assessment of immune responses as appropriate.
milestones.set_by: HHS/BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels, criterion 6C.
milestones.threshold_quote: establish an initial safety, pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity assessment as appropriate.

milestones.title: Controlled studies assess the carrier's efficacy and short-term risks in patients with hemorrhage.
milestones.criterion: Complete controlled human studies evaluating effectiveness for the intended hemorrhage indication and determining the common short-term side effects and risks in patients with the condition.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(b), definition of phase 2 investigations.
milestones.threshold_quote: evaluate the effectiveness of the drug for a particular indication or indications

milestones.title: A pivotal hemorrhage trial meets its prespecified efficacy endpoint in the primary analysis.
milestones.criterion: Meet the candidate's pivotal trial endpoint in the analysis population specified by its protocol. For PolyHeme, the endpoint was 30-day mortality among randomized and treated patients analyzed as assigned. The protocol tested superiority or noninferiority to control. For noninferiority, the upper confidence limit on mortality with PolyHeme minus mortality with control could be at most seven percentage points.
milestones.set_by: The individual pivotal trial protocol. Northfield Laboratories' PolyHeme phase III protocol supplies the mortality example.
milestones.threshold_quote: The margin to assess noninferiority, using the upper limit of the confidence interval, was set at 7% more than control.

milestones.title: The candidate takes up and releases oxygen in vitro.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate oxygen uptake and release by the candidate formulation in a laboratory assay. This is the oxygen-transport activity corresponding to HHS/BARDA criterion 3B.
milestones.set_by: HHS/BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels, criterion 3B, applied to oxygen transport.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate in vitro activity of candidate(s)

milestones.title: The carrier's preclinical safety and efficacy are within 10% of the comparable blood component.
milestones.criterion: At RAPIID Phase 1 month 6, compare the individual oxygen carrier with the corresponding blood component in vitro, in a living-animal hemorrhage model, or both. Demonstrate safety and efficacy within a 10% performance margin on justified attributes relevant to the intended use.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, RAPIID solicitation DARPA-PS-26-124, Amendment 1, TA-1, Table 2 and month 6 safety and efficacy report.
milestones.threshold_quote: within 10% margin of performance of the comparable blood component

milestones.title: The carrier stays within 10% of fresh product after six months at each of 4, 25 and 40 °C.
milestones.criterion: At RAPIID Phase 1 month 12, demonstrate at least six months of storage at each sustained temperature of 4, 25 and 40 °C with no more than 10% difference in physicochemical characteristics and functionality from unstored product of the same composition. Demonstrate the same tolerance at each temperature for at least three months in the government-chosen final packaging.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, RAPIID solicitation DARPA-PS-26-124, Amendment 1, TA-1, Table 2 and month 12 shelf-stability reports.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate ≥6 months shelf-stability at 4, 25, and 40°C with ≤10% difference in physicochemical characteristics and functionality vs. fresh product

milestones.title: The carrier demonstrates non-toxicity and pharmacological safety in preclinical assessments.
milestones.criterion: At RAPIID Phase 1 month 12, demonstrate non-toxicity and pharmacological safety of the individual oxygen carrier in the assessments supporting an Investigational New Drug application.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, RAPIID solicitation DARPA-PS-26-124, Amendment 1, TA-1, Table 2.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demonstrate non-toxicity and pharmacological safety via IND-enabling assessments

milestones.title: The sponsor submits the oxygen carrier's marketing application to FDA for the hemorrhage indication.
milestones.criterion: Submit a New Drug Application or Biologics License Application to FDA seeking the hemorrhage indication with the proposed unrefrigerated storage conditions and expiry.
milestones.set_by: HHS/BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels, criterion 8B, applied to the indication and storage conditions sought.

not_found: No current FDA oxygen-therapeutic-specific guidance prescribing a universal human mortality margin or resuscitation dose was found.
No published result was found combining the RAPIID storage test with a successful pivotal human hemorrhage trial in one product.
No results report for the phase Ib study jRCT2051240249 was found.

results.finding: Six-hour survival was 90.9% in hemorrhagic-shock rats given stored HbV (n=11).
results.detail: The study detected no significant survival difference among the transfusion groups.
results.quote: A higher 6-hour survival rate was found in the HbV group (90.9%). However, no significant difference was found among the groups.

results.finding: Six-hour survival was 7.6 percentage points higher with stored HbV (n=11) than with fresh packed red cells (n=12).
results.detail: The survival difference is calculated from the reported point estimates. The study tested for differences and did not test equivalence within a 10% margin.
results.quote: We demonstrate herein that long-term stored HbV functions as a resuscitative fluid in hemorrhagic shock model rats and that it is comparable to fresh PRBC.

results.finding: HbV retained resuscitation activity in hemorrhagic-shock rats (n=11) after one year at 4 °C.
results.detail: The fresh comparator was packed red cells. The paper attributes the multitemperature physicochemical stability findings to prior work.
results.quote: The findings reported herein indicate that 1-year-stored HbV can effectively function as a resuscitative fluid without the induction of post-transfused lung injury

results.finding: Pulmonary leakage and edema measures were similar for HbV and fresh packed red cells at six hours (n=5 per group).
results.detail: Follow-up ended at six hours, leaving longer-term post-transfusion safety unassessed.
results.quote: whereas the values for the HbV group were similar to those for the PRBC-0 group

results.finding: Hemoglobin vesicles in saline (sample size unreported) had a reported P50 of approximately 15 Torr.
results.detail: The paper does not reconcile the different P50 values in the abstract and preparation section.

results.finding: Hemoglobin vesicles restored oxygen delivery after hemorrhage in beagles (n = 4 per arm), with higher delivery than albumin alone (P < 0.0001).
results.quote:
Oxygen delivery was restored in the HbV group 
and was significantly higher than that in the HSA group (P < 0.0001).

results.finding: VS-101 achieved 67% survival at the end of observation in a rat hemorrhage study (36 rats, 9 per arm).
results.detail: The VS-101 group was about 13% heavier than the other groups. Hemorrhage and infusion volumes were scaled to body weight.
results.quote: with 67% of animals surviving the full 8-h observation phase while no other group had survivors at 8 h

results.finding: VS-101 produced twice the peripheral tissue oxygen tension of whole blood after hemorrhage (9 rats per arm at enrollment).
results.detail: The twofold difference was recorded 180 minutes after resuscitation. Mortality limited comparisons at later time points.
results.quote:

results.finding: VS-101 caused no observed systemic hypertension or arteriolar vasoconstriction in 9 treated rats monitored for up to 8 hours.
results.detail: The authors called for further toxicology in larger cohorts, in both sexes, across animal species, and at higher doses.
results.quote: Neither arteriolar vasoconstriction nor hypertension was noted

results.finding: YQ23 formulation (sample size unreported) had an oxygen p50 of approximately 40 mmHg.
results.quote: The pH of the product in this study ranged from 7.3 to 7.6, and the p50 was approximately 40 mmHg.

results.finding: Rats with uncontrolled hemorrhagic shock receiving 5% YQ23 (n=16/group) had a median survival of 14.8 hours.
results.detail: Miniature pigs also showed improved oxygen delivery and utilization, with six animals per group.
results.quote: The results showed that YQ23 could prolong the survival time of rats compared with LR, there were 6/16 and 8/16 rats that survived over 12 h in 2 and 5% YQ23 group, respectively, and the median survival time was 8.5 and 14.8 h.

results.finding: In hemorrhagic rats (n=16/group), mean blood loss with 5% YQ23 was 2.6% lower than with whole blood plus lactated Ringer’s.
results.detail: The 2.6% is calculated from the reported group means. It describes a single outcome and does not establish equivalence.
results.quote: the blood loss proportion was 45.38 ± 4.08%, 46.58 ± 4.50% and 62.33 ± 3.93% in 5% YQ23, WB + LR and LR group, respectively,

results.finding: YQ23 resuscitation in hemorrhagic rats (n=10/group per time point) and pigs (n=6/group) showed no observed renal injury.
results.detail: The study collected organ-injury markers through two hours after treatment. Coagulopathy and hemostasis effects remained unknown.
results.quote: Side effects such as vasoconstriction and renal injury were not observed.

results.finding: The NMU-HbV phase 1 trial began in October 2020 after PMDA agreement and trial review committee approval. Participant count unreported.
results.detail: The universities’ release describes the agreement and approval. It supplies no regulator decision or committee record.

results.finding: In the NMU-HbV phase 1 trial, the 100 mL cohort had an estimated half-life of about 8 hours. Cohort size unreported.
results.detail: The highest-dose cohort received dexamethasone, famotidine and acetaminophen before infusion. The release identifies the peer-reviewed Blood Advances article that reports the phase 1 results.

results.finding: HbV-101 received Japanese regulatory and ethics approval for a phase 1 trial with 12 planned volunteers.
results.quote:
The protocol (HbV-101) was approved by Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency and the local
ethical committee (institutional review board) of Hokkaido University (registration number,

results.finding: Hemoglobin vesicles had a mean circulating half-life of 8.2 hours in the two volunteers who completed the highest-dose infusion.
results.detail: One infusion was halted after a rash with a wheal. The fourth participant in that cohort went undosed because pandemic-related rescheduling and expiry of the investigational product ended the cohort.
results.quote:
Pharmacokinetic analysis results revealed that HbVs circulate in the
bloodstream with a half-life of approximately 8 hours ( Figure 2 C).

results.finding: In 44 randomized trauma patients, PolyHeme reduced mean donor red-cell use by 3.6 units through day 1.
results.detail: The 3.6-unit reduction is calculated from the reported group means. The day 3 comparison had p = 0.06.
results.quote: The total number of allogeneic red cell transfusions for the control and experimental groups was 10.4+/-4.2 units vs. 6.8+/-3.9 units (p < 0.05) through day 1, and 11.3+/-4.1 units vs. 7.8 +/-4.2 units (p = 0.06) through day 3.

results.finding: Pilot-scale unencapsulated tense-state polymerized human hemoglobin (n = 3 batches) released oxygen in vitro at 32.7 ± 8.6 s⁻¹.
results.detail: P50 is the oxygen partial pressure at half saturation. The stopped-flow assay measured oxygen dissociation after rapid mixing of the oxygenated formulation with sodium dithionite in degassed buffer. Table 1 reports means ± standard deviations.

results.finding: In 16 beagles (8 per group), perfluorochemical emulsion restored mixed venous PO2 to preshock values for 60 minutes.
results.detail: Hemodynamic variables remained abnormal in both groups. The difference in 3-hour survival was statistically nonsignificant.
results.quote: Mixed venous PO2 returned to preshock values in the perfluorochemical-treated dogs for 60 mins after fluid administration (p < .01).

results.finding: In the swine hemorrhage model, 4 of 6 HBOC-201 recipients had mild to moderate liver injury.
results.detail: The matched-pressure arms targeted a mean arterial pressure of 60 mm Hg for four hours. Liver histology at day 3 showed a 66.7-percentage-point excess in injury incidence with HBOC-201 versus shed whole blood.
results.quote:
Mild to moderate degeneration and/or necrosis of centri-
lobular to midzonal hepatocytes was observed in four of six
animals in the HBOC (60) group (Fig. 9 A and B) and one of
six animals in the LR /H11001 Blood group.

results.finding: PEG-modified, deoxygenated hemoglobin vesicles showed 4% total hemoglobin leakage after one year at 40 °C (one sample described).
results.detail: The 4% leakage measures only one aspect of stability. At 40 °C the sample also showed precipitation, vesicle component decomposition and a drop in pH.
results.quote: the sample stored at 40 °C showed the precipitation and decomposition of vesicular components, a decrease in pH, and 4% leakage of total Hb after 1 year.

results.finding: Dodecafluoropentane emulsion (sample size unreported) averaged <400 nm in particle size after six months at room temperature.
results.quote: The average particle size of the dodecafluoropentane emulsion is < 400 nm stored at room temperature for 6 months.

results.finding: Oxygen-bound hemoglobin vesicles (6 rats per dose) showed no observed neurobehavioral toxicity versus saline through 72 hours after IV infusion.
results.detail: Behavioral and sensory-reflex observations were descriptive. The reported day-14 brain histology covered carbon monoxide-bound vesicles and saline controls.
results.quote:
No toxicological effect was observed in any measurement item for any
group in comparison to the control saline infusion group.

results.finding: Perflubron emulsion phase 1 studies enrolled 48 healthy volunteers and found a 9.4-hour intravascular half-life at the higher dose.
results.detail: The half-life estimate covers the first 24 hours after infusion. The higher-dose platelet count reduction resolved by day 7.
results.quote: The intravascular half-life of perflubron for the first 24 h was dose dependent: 9.4+/-2.2 h and 6.1+/-1.9 h in the 1.8- and 1.2-g PFC/kg groups, respectively.

results.finding: In a randomized PolyHeme trial for traumatic hemorrhagic shock (n = 714), 93% of PolyHeme recipients had a reported adverse event.
results.detail: The control group had access to red cells after hospital arrival, so the trial directly evaluated prehospital use and used the first 12 hours of PolyHeme treatment to simulate a longer delay in access to blood.
results.quote: As expected in seriously injured patients, AEs were reported in virtually all: 93% (324/349) of PolyHeme patients and 88% (322/365) of Control patients

results.finding: Fluosol DA-20 transiently increased dissolved oxygen content after recent bleeding (46 patients, 36 randomized, p < 0.02).
results.detail: The efficacy signal was a transient change in dissolved oxygen content. The mortality comparison was nonsignificant, and the reported infusion tolerability applied to patients with a negative test dose.
results.quote: The plasma or dissolved component of oxygen content was significantly higher in the FDA group at 12 h (FDA group 1.58 +/- 0.47 ml/dl, control group 1.01 +/- 0.31 ml/dl, p less than .02, t-test).

case_label = "Carrier formulation". Reason: Carrier formulation identifies which products can be compared when interpreting the animal and clinical results.

definition = "An intravenous fluid carries oxygen to tissues during life-threatening hemorrhage when donor red cells are unavailable. Its labelled storage conditions allow stocking without refrigeration, and it can be given without matching the patient's blood group. It supplies the oxygen-delivery function of red cells. Platelets and clotting factors serve separate functions. Hemopure, made from the oxygen-carrying protein hemoglobin, already keeps at room temperature for at least three years. Its South African approval covers acute anemia in adult surgical patients, and its US use remains investigational.". Reason: Hemopure already provides unrefrigerated storage, so the definition needs to identify the hemorrhage indication and distinguish oxygen support from replacement of whole blood.

goal.need = "In US emergency medical services records for 2020\u20132023, only 2,289 of 262,761 injured patients who met a vital-sign screen for possible transfusion received blood before hospital arrival. Donor red cells in additive solutions ordinarily keep for 42 days at 1\u20136 \u00b0C. Where crews cannot maintain refrigeration, a safe oxygen carrier could support a bleeding patient's tissues during transport until donor red cells are available. Patients still need bleeding control and may need platelets and clotting factors.". Reason: The existing paragraph gives the storage limit but omits the measured gap in prehospital transfusion and what a patient would still need during bleeding.

add statement by Institute of Medicine, Committee on Fluid Resuscitation for Combat Casualties, 1999: "delivery in the wounded subject for 24 to 48 hours.". Reason: Recommendation 4.1 identifies an independent academy committee that set a duration of oxygen support worth investigating.

edit completion: basis = "HHS/BARDA uses FDA approval or licensure as its threshold and requires stability studies to support labelled expiry. The indication, dose and storage conditions belong to the individual product. Fluosol's US approval covered myocardial ischemia during coronary angioplasty. Hemopure has South African approval for acute anemia in adult surgical patients and remains investigational in the US, including under expanded access. FDA withdrew its oxygen-therapeutics draft guidance on 8 May 2015."; refs = [4, 5, 6, 21, 25, 26]. Reason: The existing basis covers hemoglobin carriers but omits the US approval of a perfluorochemical for another indication and the investigational status of room-temperature Hemopure.
add case "Unencapsulated hemoglobin". Reason: PolyHeme and Hemopure use hemoglobin in solution, and their clinical results concern that formulation.
add case "Encapsulated hemoglobin". Reason: Hemoglobin vesicles enclose the protein in a membrane and have their own hemorrhage studies and human safety evidence.
add case "Perfluorocarbon emulsion". Reason: Perfluorocarbon emulsions form a separate family of oxygen carriers with a distinct clinical record.
add milestone after None: "The candidate takes up and releases oxygen in vitro.". Reason: The sequence starts in animals and skips the laboratory demonstration of the carrier's intended activity.

edit m1: criterion = "Demonstrate preliminary efficacy of the candidate as a resuscitation fluid in a living-animal model of hemorrhage. Good Laboratory Practice compliance is not required for this proof-of-concept study."; set_by = "HHS/BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels, criterion 3C."; threshold_quote = "Generate preliminary in vivo proof-of-concept efficacy data"; threshold_ref = 4; refs = [4, 7, 8]. Reason: The criterion mixes animal outcomes with the test and equates one proof-of-concept activity with the entire readiness level.

split m2 into "The carrier's preclinical safety and efficacy are within 10% of the comparable blood component." | "The carrier stays within 10% of fresh product after six months at each of 4, 25 and 40 °C." | "The carrier demonstrates non-toxicity and pharmacological safety in preclinical assessments.". Reason: RAPIID measures comparative performance, storage stability and toxicology separately, so each can be judged from the evidence that tests it.

edit m3: criterion = "Meet the regulatory and ethics requirements to begin the human investigation in its jurisdiction. Institutional review board approval is also required. An investigation under the emergency research exception from informed consent requires prior written FDA authorization."; set_by = "FDA, 21 CFR 312.40 and 312.20(c), for the US route."; threshold_quote = "Thirty days after FDA receives the IND"; threshold_ref = 10; refs = [10, 11, 12]. Reason: The Japanese study is evidence for the milestone, while the criterion needs to specify what permits a trial to begin in the applicable jurisdiction.

edit m4: criterion = "Complete one or more phase 1 trials that establish initial human safety and pharmacokinetics for the candidate, with assessment of immune responses as appropriate."; set_by = "HHS/BARDA, Integrated Technology Readiness Levels, criterion 6C."; threshold_quote = "establish an initial safety, pharmacokinetics and immunogenicity assessment as appropriate."; threshold_ref = 4; refs = [4, 12, 13, 14]. Reason: Volunteer counts, adverse events and a later protocol's planned doses obscure the test for a completed initial human assessment.

edit m5: title = "Controlled studies assess the carrier's efficacy and short-term risks in patients with hemorrhage."; criterion = "Complete controlled human studies evaluating effectiveness for the intended hemorrhage indication and determining the common short-term side effects and risks in patients with the condition."; set_by = "FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(b), definition of phase 2 investigations."; threshold_quote = "evaluate the effectiveness of the drug for a particular indication or indications"; threshold_ref = 11; refs = [11, 15]. Reason: FDA defines phase 2 by the evaluation performed, whereas the title implies a positive efficacy finding and the criterion reports one trial's transfusion counts.

edit m6: title = "A pivotal hemorrhage trial meets its prespecified efficacy endpoint in the primary analysis."; criterion = "Meet the candidate's pivotal trial endpoint in the analysis population specified by its protocol. For PolyHeme, the endpoint was 30-day mortality among randomized and treated patients analyzed as assigned. The protocol tested superiority or noninferiority to control. For noninferiority, the upper confidence limit on mortality with PolyHeme minus mortality with control could be at most seven percentage points."; set_by = "The individual pivotal trial protocol. Northfield Laboratories' PolyHeme phase III protocol supplies the mortality example."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "The margin to assess noninferiority, using the upper limit of the confidence interval, was set at 7% more than control."; threshold_ref = 16; refs = [16]. Reason: The pivotal test must distinguish the prespecified primary analysis from secondary analyses and keep PolyHeme's seven-point margin specific to its protocol.

add milestone after m6: "The sponsor submits the oxygen carrier's marketing application to FDA for the hemorrhage indication.". Reason: HHS/BARDA identifies submission of the marketing application as a distinct step between pivotal evidence and FDA approval.
